companies.name: Novaxis Chips
companies.desc: The market's largest company: it designs the processors and memory used in data centres, computers and connected devices, and has them made by outside foundries. Demand for AI computing drives its sales.

companies.name: CloudRail
companies.desc: Rents out computing, storage and software tools from its cloud data centres to businesses moving online. Customers pay as they go, so its revenue grows with their usage.

companies.name: ByteForge AI
companies.desc: Builds AI models and the computing systems used to train and run them, sold to businesses as a service. It spends heavily on research and computing power.

companies.name: SolarGrid
companies.desc: Builds and owns large solar farms with batteries and sells their power to grid operators under twenty-year contracts. It borrows heavily to build, so interest rates matter to it as much as sunshine.

companies.name: Ostrava Oil
companies.desc: An integrated oil major: it finds and pumps crude oil and gas, moves them through its own pipelines and refines them into fuels for airlines, power plants and industry. Its profit follows the oil price, and it pays a large dividend.

companies.name: Helix Biolabs
companies.desc: A clinical-stage biotech testing antibody drugs for immune disorders such as lupus. It has no product on sale yet, so its value rests on trial results.

companies.name: CuraGen
companies.desc: Makes established prescription medicines for heart disease, diabetes and infections, plus low-cost generics, sold to pharmacies and hospitals. A steady earner, it must keep replacing drugs whose patents expire.

companies.name: Aegis Dynamics
companies.desc: A prime defense contractor that builds radar systems and secure military communications and maintains aircraft for governments. Its contracts run for decades, so revenue is very predictable and depends mainly on defense budgets.

companies.name: SkyJet Airways
companies.desc: A full-service national airline with two hub airports, long-haul international routes and a frequent-flyer programme that earns money from credit-card partners. Profits swing with ticket demand, and fuel is its biggest cost after wages.

companies.name: Munchly Foods
companies.desc: Makes frozen meals, pasta sauces and pantry staples under a dozen household brands, plus own-label goods for supermarkets. People buy them in good times and bad, which makes it one of the steadiest stocks on the market.

companies.name: ZipDrop Delivery
companies.desc: Delivers groceries, takeaways and parcels from local shops within the hour, using gig couriers on bikes and vans. It charges shops a commission and customers a fee, and is barely profitable.

companies.name: Bankr Holdings
companies.desc: The largest bank on the market: current accounts, mortgages, business loans and card payments for millions of customers. It earns the gap between what it pays on deposits and what it charges on loans, so interest rates and defaults drive its profit.

companies.name: Steady Bonds
companies.desc: A short-duration government bond fund designed to hold value when riskier assets are unsettled.

companies.name: Golden Reserve
companies.desc: A gold-backed trust whose shares track bullion prices and investor demand for a defensive asset.

companies.name: DOGO Inc
companies.desc: Owns a cartoon dog that went viral and sells the merchandise, licences and fan events built around it. Almost all of its value rests on online attention, so its price swings with every trend and meme.

companies.name: Moon Rockets
companies.desc: A small rocket start-up that has flown twice and is chasing contracts to launch cheap small satellites. It has little revenue, burns cash on every test, and its fans trade it on hope.
